item.title: Autistic Self-Compassion Begins Here
item.description:
Autism

Autistic Self-Compassion Begins Here

Replacing self-blame with understanding, acceptance, and hope.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic people's mental health issues are sometimes linked to how they view past experiences.
  • An autism diagnosis can help people reinterpret their lives with greater understanding and self compassion.
  • Self judgement often develops from misunderstanding autistic differences rather than personal failings.
  • Viewing the past through an autistic lens can support healing and improve well-being.

When I went to my GP to ask about an autism assessment, several years ago now, he asked me what I felt I would gain from it. Amongst other things, including seeking out the right type of therapeutic support and having clear self-care measures in place, I told him it would help me make sense of my life up to that point.

For context, it was a life filled with questionable decisions, failed relationships, and a very chequered job history. It felt like a life of unfulfilled potential, characterised by uncertainty and doubt, through which I'd somehow ploughed with anxiety, OCD, and eating disorders. All of these things had affected my self-esteem, and I felt that an autism diagnosis, by helping me understand those experiences, would allow me to offer myself self-compassion based on deep understanding.

Autistic woman reflecting on her past
Source: zoro-too-images, Canva

I can understand why this was at odds with what the GP was asking. He was working in the world of illness and injury, and, as our brief conversation revealed, he saw neurodevelopmental conditions from the perspective of support needs and medication. But for me, understanding my past and being able to look back with awareness and compassion has been one of the most significant outcomes of my diagnosis.

I'm not alone. Catherine, a client in her late sixties, cited this as the most important reason for having an assessment. "There's a part of me that thinks I'm ridiculous for pursuing this," she told me. "I'm retired, I don't need help at work. I've even found better ways of managing my mental health. But I want to know. I feel haunted by some of the things I've done in the past. I just want to look back and understand why, and be a bit kinder to myself."

Emily's reasons for seeking out a diagnosis in her late forties were similar, but straddled that intersection between making sense of the past with a view to moving forward in a new relationship and repairing her relationship with her adult children. Emily had been unable to cope with motherhood earlier in her life and had left the family home, where her ex partner raised their children. "I have felt this horrific guilt every day, even though I've always retained a relationship with my kids," she told me. "I want that relationship to be stronger going forward, and I feel that, although I'll always have some guilt about leaving, knowing I'm autistic will allow me to be a bit more compassionate towards my younger self. I feel the guilt's become a barrier between us, and I need to let go of it to rebuild our relationship."

Having an autism diagnosis doesn't lead to an overnight shift in how you view your younger self, but it can offer a very significant starting point in moving towards a new perspective. Many people find they move from a critical, often harsh assessment of their past actions and choices towards a far more empathic understanding of themselves as someone who made choices from a difficult place.

Chantelle used her diagnosis as the catalyst for working with a therapist who specialised in inner child therapy. "For the first time, I didn't see myself as a bad child," she shared. "I realised I was a misunderstood little girl, struggling to make sense of things, experiencing severe meltdowns because I was pushed into situations which I couldn't tolerate. I spent a lot of years thinking that everything I was told about my tantrums, about being naughty, about being disruptive and bad, was right. And it made me hate myself. Now, I'm learning a completely new way to look at that younger self, which is at the root of my healing and recovery."

If we return, for a moment, to the more practical view of neurodivergence that some healthcare professionals might take, including thinking about neurodevelopmental conditions in relation to support needs, we can begin to see the link between bringing self compassion to our past selves and meeting our current needs. There is a significant association between autism and mental health conditions, including anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation. However, in my experience of working with thousands of autistic adults, much of this distress stems from years of misunderstanding ourselves, judging ourselves against neurotypical expectations, and believing that our struggles reflected personal failings rather than genuine differences in the way our minds work. Looking back on those experiences with self compassion allows us to replace self blame with understanding, while also helping us recognise and respond more effectively to the needs we have in the present.

Understanding our past is not about excusing every decision we've made or becoming stuck in what has already happened. It's about recognising that we can only make sense of our lives through the knowledge we have at the time. When that understanding changes, it becomes possible to view ourselves differently, and that shift in perspective can shape the choices we make from this point onwards.
